elements.name: Write-Ahead Log
elements.what: Append every intended change to a sequential durable log and force it to stable storage before the corresponding in-place data update, so committed work can be redone and uncommitted work undone after a crash.
elements.problem: In-place updates can be half-applied when a crash hits; sequential logging makes durability cheap (one sequential write) and gives recovery a total order of changes to replay or roll back.
elements.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

elements.name: Checkpointing
elements.what: Periodically record a consistent marker of which logged changes have reached the main data store, bounding how far back crash recovery must scan the log.
elements.problem: Without checkpoints the recovery log grows without bound and restart must replay the whole history; a checkpoint truncates the redo horizon and caps recovery time.
elements.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

elements.name: Group Commit
elements.what: Accumulate the log records of several concurrently committing transactions and flush them to stable storage with a single synchronous write.
elements.problem: One fsync per commit makes the log device the throughput ceiling; amortizing one flush over many commits trades a little latency for large gains in commit throughput.
elements.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

elements.name: Shadow Paging
elements.what: Perform updates on copies of pages and atomically switch a page-table root from the old (shadow) versions to the new ones at commit, never overwriting committed state in place.
elements.problem: Gives atomic, no-log crash recovery: a crash before the root switch leaves the intact shadow state; the cost is copying pressure and lost clustering, the classic alternative to write-ahead logging.
elements.named_in: Physical Integrity in a Large Segmented Database - Lorie (1977)

elements.name: Copy-on-Write B-Tree
elements.what: A B-tree whose updates never modify pages in place: changed pages and their ancestors up to the root are rewritten to new locations, and commit is an atomic root swap.
elements.problem: Combines B-tree lookup with crash safety and lock-free readers (old roots stay valid snapshots) without a separate recovery log; used by LMDB and btrfs at the cost of write amplification.
elements.named_in: Database Internals - Petrov (2019)

elements.name: Buffer Pool
elements.what: A fixed set of in-memory frames that caches disk pages, tracks pin counts and dirty state, and mediates all page reads and writes between the storage layer and disk.
elements.problem: Disk access is orders of magnitude slower than memory; a managed page cache exploits locality while controlling exactly when dirty pages reach disk, which the recovery protocol depends on (steal/force policies).
elements.named_in: Architecture of a Database System - Hellerstein, Stonebraker & Hamilton (2007)

elements.name: Slotted Page Layout
elements.what: A page format with a slot directory growing from one end and variable-length records growing from the other, so records are addressed by stable slot number rather than byte offset.
elements.problem: Variable-length records must be inserted, deleted, and relocated within a fixed-size page without invalidating external record identifiers; the indirection slot array permits in-page compaction while record ids stay stable.
elements.named_in: Database Internals - Petrov (2019)

elements.name: Log-Structured Merge-Tree
elements.what: A write-optimized index that absorbs writes in an in-memory sorted structure (memtable), flushes it as immutable sorted runs on disk (SSTables), and background-merges runs (compaction) to bound read cost.
elements.problem: In-place trees pay a random write per update; converting random writes into sequential flushes plus deferred merging trades read and space amplification for far higher sustained write throughput.
elements.named_in: The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree) - O'Neil, Cheng, Gawlick & O'Neil (1996)

elements.name: Multiversion Concurrency Control
elements.what: Keep multiple timestamped versions of each data item so readers see a consistent older version while writers create new ones, with obsolete versions garbage-collected later.
elements.problem: Lock-based schemes make readers and writers block each other; versioning lets reads proceed without locks against a stable snapshot at the cost of version storage and cleanup (vacuum).
elements.named_in: Multiversion Concurrency Control - Theory and Algorithms - Bernstein & Goodman (1983)

elements.name: Snapshot Isolation
elements.what: A transaction reads from a consistent snapshot taken at its start and commits only if no concurrent committed transaction wrote the same items (first-committer-wins).
elements.problem: Gives long-running reads a stable, non-blocking view while catching write-write conflicts; weaker than serializability (admits write skew), which is exactly the trade-off it names.
elements.named_in: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels - Berenson, Bernstein, Gray, Melton, O'Neil & O'Neil (1995)
elements.borderline: Primarily an isolation-level semantics; included because it names the concrete snapshot-read + first-committer-wins mechanism MVCC engines implement.

elements.name: Two-Phase Locking
elements.what: A locking discipline in which a transaction acquires all its locks before releasing any (growing then shrinking phase), which suffices to guarantee serializable executions.
elements.problem: Ad-hoc lock acquisition and release admits non-serializable interleavings; the two-phase rule is the classic protocol-level fix, at the price of blocking and possible deadlock.
elements.named_in: The Notions of Consistency and Predicate Locks in a Database System - Eswaran, Gray, Lorie & Traiger (1976)

elements.name: Optimistic Concurrency Control
elements.what: Execute transactions without locks against private working copies, then validate at commit that no conflicting concurrent access occurred, aborting and retrying on conflict.
elements.problem: When conflicts are rare, pessimistic locking pays overhead and blocking for protection it seldom needs; optimistic validation moves the cost to the (rare) conflict case.
elements.named_in: On Optimistic Methods for Concurrency Control - Kung & Robinson (1981)

elements.name: Timestamp-Ordering Concurrency Control
elements.what: Assign each transaction a unique timestamp at start and enforce that all conflicting reads and writes execute in timestamp order, aborting operations that arrive too late.
elements.problem: Provides serializability without locks or deadlocks by pre-deciding the serialization order; the third classic concurrency-control family alongside 2PL and OCC.
elements.named_in: Concurrency Control in Distributed Database Systems - Bernstein & Goodman (1981)

elements.name: Multi-Granularity Locking
elements.what: Locks are taken at multiple granularities (database, table, page, row) with intention modes (IS, IX, SIX) on ancestors advertising finer-grained locks below.
elements.problem: Row-only locking makes whole-table operations acquire millions of locks, while table-only locking kills concurrency; the intention-mode hierarchy lets both coexist with cheap conflict checks.
elements.named_in: Granularity of Locks and Degrees of Consistency in a Shared Data Base - Gray, Lorie, Putzolu & Traiger (1976)

elements.name: Lock Escalation
elements.what: When a transaction holds too many fine-grained locks, the lock manager replaces them with a single coarser-granularity lock to cap lock-table memory.
elements.problem: Fine-grained locking has per-lock overhead that can exhaust the lock table; escalation trades concurrency for bounded lock-manager resources.
elements.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)
elements.borderline: A resource-bounding policy inside the lock manager rather than a standalone mechanism; included as it is named, recurring, and independently implementable.

elements.name: Deadlock Detection
elements.what: Maintain a waits-for graph of which transactions block which, periodically detect cycles, and break them by aborting a chosen victim (alternatives: timeouts, wound-wait/wait-die prevention).
elements.problem: Blocking lock protocols can produce circular waits that never resolve; explicit detection converts a permanent hang into a bounded abort-and-retry.
elements.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

elements.name: Volcano Iterator Model
elements.what: Every query operator implements a uniform open/next/close iterator interface and pulls one tuple at a time from its children, composing arbitrary operator trees into demand-driven pipelines.
elements.problem: Operators need to compose without materializing intermediate results or knowing each other's internals; the uniform pull interface makes pipelining and operator extensibility mechanical.
elements.named_in: Volcano - An Extensible and Parallel Query Evaluation System - Graefe (1994)

elements.name: Vectorized Execution
elements.what: Query operators pass batches (vectors) of hundreds or thousands of values per next() call instead of single tuples, running tight primitive loops over each batch.
elements.problem: Tuple-at-a-time iteration pays interpretation overhead per row and defeats CPU caches and SIMD; batching amortizes dispatch cost and enables cache- and SIMD-friendly inner loops.
elements.named_in: MonetDB/X100: Hyper-Pipelining Query Execution - Boncz, Zukowski & Nes (2005)
elements.borderline: Arguably an optimization of the iterator model rather than a distinct mechanism; kept separate because the batch-interface design is independently named and adopted (DuckDB, Velox, Arrow).

elements.name: Cursor
elements.what: A named, positioned handle over a query result set that the client advances row by row (optionally scrolling or updating through it) instead of receiving the whole result at once.
elements.problem: Set-oriented query results must be consumed by record-at-a-time application code with bounded memory; the cursor bridges the set/record impedance and carries position state across calls.
elements.named_in: ISO/IEC 9075 - Database Language SQL

elements.name: Secondary Index
elements.what: An auxiliary structure mapping non-primary-key attribute values to record locations (or primary keys), maintained alongside the base data on every write.
elements.problem: Queries on attributes other than the primary access path degenerate to full scans; a redundant per-attribute index buys lookup speed at the cost of write amplification and consistency maintenance.
elements.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017)
elements.borderline: Generic 'index' altitude is contested; kept because 'secondary index' names a specific recurring design decision (redundant derived access path maintained on write).

elements.name: Column-Oriented Storage
elements.what: Store all values of each column contiguously (rather than row by row), typically with per-column compression, so queries read only the columns they touch.
elements.problem: Analytical scans over wide tables waste I/O and cache on unused columns in row layout; columnar layout minimizes bytes read and makes runs of same-typed values highly compressible and SIMD-friendly.
elements.named_in: C-Store: A Column-oriented DBMS - Stonebraker et al. (2005)

elements.name: Cache-Aside
elements.what: Application code checks the cache first, loads from the backing store on a miss, populates the cache itself, and invalidates or updates the entry when it writes the store.
elements.problem: Keeps the cache optional and the store authoritative when the cache cannot sit transparently in the data path; the application accepts responsibility for population and invalidation consistency.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft patterns & practices (2014)

elements.name: Read-Through Cache
elements.what: The cache itself, not the application, loads missing entries from the backing store via a pluggable loader when a get misses, then returns and retains the value.
elements.problem: Centralizes miss-handling so callers see one always-answering interface, and lets the cache coalesce concurrent misses for the same key (thundering-herd protection).
elements.named_in: Read-Through, Write-Through, Write-Behind, and Refresh-Ahead Caching - Oracle Coherence Developer's Guide (2009)

elements.name: Write-Through Cache
elements.what: Writes go to the cache, which synchronously propagates them to the backing store before acknowledging, keeping cache and store consistent at all times.
elements.problem: Guarantees the store never lags the cache (no dirty data to lose) at the cost of paying full store latency on every write; the safety end of the write-policy spectrum.
elements.named_in: Read-Through, Write-Through, Write-Behind, and Refresh-Ahead Caching - Oracle Coherence Developer's Guide (2009)

elements.name: Write-Behind Cache
elements.what: Writes are acknowledged once they hit the cache and are propagated to the backing store asynchronously, often batched and coalesced, after a delay.
elements.problem: Synchronous store writes cap write latency and throughput; deferring and batching them absorbs bursts and coalesces repeated writes, at the risk of losing acknowledged-but-unflushed data.
elements.named_in: Read-Through, Write-Through, Write-Behind, and Refresh-Ahead Caching - Oracle Coherence Developer's Guide (2009)

elements.name: Refresh-Ahead Cache
elements.what: When a cached entry is read close to its expiry, the cache returns the current value and asynchronously reloads a fresh one from the backing store before it expires.
elements.problem: Plain TTL expiry makes some unlucky reader pay the reload latency on hot keys; refreshing ahead of expiry hides reload cost for frequently accessed entries.
elements.named_in: Read-Through, Write-Through, Write-Behind, and Refresh-Ahead Caching - Oracle Coherence Developer's Guide (2009)

elements.name: Cache Eviction Policy
elements.what: The rule a bounded cache uses to choose which resident entry to discard when admitting a new one, approximating 'least likely to be needed again' (recency-, frequency-, or clock-based).
elements.problem: A cache smaller than its working set must evict; the choice of victim policy determines hit rate and scan-resistance and is a named, pluggable design decision in every cache and buffer pool.
elements.named_in: Database Internals - Petrov (2019)

elements.name: Prefetching
elements.what: Fetch data into a cache or buffer before it is requested, based on a predicted access pattern (most commonly sequential readahead), overlapping fetch latency with useful work.
elements.problem: Demand fetching stalls the consumer for the full miss latency; when the access pattern is predictable, speculatively issuing fetches early hides that latency at the risk of wasted bandwidth on wrong guesses.
elements.named_in: Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach - Hennessy & Patterson (1990)

parked_architecture.name: Two-phase commit (2PC)
parked_architecture.why: Atomic commit protocol coordinating multiple independent participants across a system - a distributed/system-structure protocol, not a single-component mechanism (Gray & Reuter name it; Phase 3 candidate).

parked_architecture.name: Log shipping / replication log (primary-replica replication)
parked_architecture.why: Reuses the WAL as a system-level replication channel between nodes - statement of system structure, feeds Phase 3 (named in Kleppmann DDIA).

parked_architecture.name: Shared-nothing parallel database architecture
parked_architecture.why: Whole-system partitioning/topology decision (Stonebraker 1986 'The Case for Shared Nothing') - clearly architecture realm.

parked_architecture.name: Partitioning / sharding
parked_architecture.why: Distribution of a dataset across nodes is system-level structure (DDIA ch. 6); the in-component analogue (hash partitioning of an in-memory structure) would be a different, unnamed-at-this-altitude candidate.

parked_architecture.name: Query optimizer / query planner
parked_architecture.why: Named recurring construct but primarily a component role in DBMS system structure (Hellerstein et al. 2007 anatomy) rather than a reusable design mechanism; parked rather than dropped.

excluded_notable.name: Join algorithms (nested-loop, sort-merge, hash join, grace/hybrid hash)
excluded_notable.why: Excluded per charter: algorithm zoo at algorithmics granularity - datastructures corpus territory; the execution-model elements (Volcano, vectorized) carry the design-level content.

excluded_notable.name: ARIES
excluded_notable.why: A specific published recovery algorithm (Mohan et al. 1992), not a distinct design element - its ideas (WAL, fuzzy checkpointing, redo/undo passes) are folded into the write-ahead-log and checkpointing entries.

excluded_notable.name: Latch
excluded_notable.why: DB-internals name for a short-term lightweight mutex on in-memory structures (Hellerstein et al. 2007 distinguishes locks vs latches); folds into the generic mutex/lock element owned by the concurrency scout - recorded so the aka is not lost.

excluded_notable.name: ACID properties / SQL isolation levels (read committed, repeatable read, serializable)
excluded_notable.why: Correctness semantics and contract taxonomy, not implementable mechanisms (Haerder & Reuter 1983; Berenson et al. 1995); snapshot isolation alone was admitted as the mechanism-shaped borderline.

excluded_notable.name: Steal/no-steal, force/no-force buffer policies
excluded_notable.why: A 2x2 policy taxonomy for buffer-pool/recovery interaction (Haerder & Reuter 1983), noted under buffer-pool and write-ahead-log rather than as standalone elements.

excluded_notable.name: Write amplification / read amplification / space amplification
excluded_notable.why: Named evaluation metrics for storage designs (RUM conjecture), not mechanisms.

excluded_notable.name: Predicate locking
excluded_notable.why: Named in Eswaran et al. 1976 but essentially a (rarely implemented) generalization within the 2PL family; folded as a note under two-phase-locking rather than a separate element.

notes: Coverage: 28 elements across persistence-durability (4), data-structures (3), data-representation (2), synchronization-coordination (8), data-flow-buffering (3), caching-memoization (8). Fold decisions logged per charter: (1) undo/redo logging FOLDED into write-ahead-log (aka + what) - Gray & Reuter treat undo/redo as roles of the single WAL protocol, and ARIES (the redo/undo realization) is excluded_notable as an algorithm; (2) memtable + SSTable FOLDED under lsm-tree as aka - DDIA and the Bigtable paper (Chang et al. 2006) name them, but they are constituent parts of one mechanism, and compaction is carried in the lsm-tree what/problem as a note rather than a separate element; (3) cache eviction policy kept as ONE element with LRU/LFU/CLOCK/2Q/LRU-K/ARC as aka - the variants are the algorithmics zoo (datastructures corpus territory), the pluggable-victim-policy slot is the design element; (4) the four Coherence caching strategies (read-through/write-through/write-behind/refresh-ahead) kept as SEPARATE elements plus cache-aside (Microsoft Cloud Design Patterns) - each names a distinct data-path/consistency contract, matching charter enumeration; write-back folded into write-behind as aka (Hennessy & Patterson CPU-cache usage). Spot-checks this session: Oracle Coherence doc section title 'Read-Through, Write-Through, Write-Behind, and Refresh-Ahead Caching' confirmed live (docs.oracle.com, Coherence 3.5 Developer's Guide); Petrov Database Internals confirmed live to contain 'Slotted Pages' (ch. 4 Implementing B-Trees) and Copy-on-Write B-tree variants (ch. 6 B-Tree Variants) via O'Reilly TOC. No db-internals naming sources exist in the corpus work-id map (checked: no Kleppmann/Petrov/Hellerstein/Gray-Reuter entries), so all named_in_corpus_id are null - Phase 2 will need DDIA, Database Internals, Architecture of a Database System, and Transaction Processing as new nodes. Thin spots for other scouts / later sweeps: plain B-tree/B+tree, bloom filter, skip list (datastructures scout); distributed-transactions and replication vocabulary parked for Phase 3; query-optimization vocabulary (cost model, cardinality estimation) deliberately left out as component-internal algorithmics; bitmap index / inverted index / zone maps could extend the index family if a later sweep wants deeper index coverage.
